claims.text: The starting material is single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a closely related chemically disordered high-entropy derivative.
Annealing at approximately 550 °C for 2–3 hours followed by controlled cooling will induce partial atomic ordering in the starting alloy.
Approximately 550 °C is below the disorder–order transition of the proposed FeCoNi material.
The proposed annealing window will produce short-range-ordered regions while avoiding complete ordering and secondary-phase formation.
Short-range ordering modifies local symmetry and increases local magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Short-range-ordered regions act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Enhanced magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain-wall pinning will increase coercivity.
The annealed material will have a coercive field greater than 100 Oe.
The annealed material will retain saturation magnetization similar to that of the untreated fcc alloy.
The untreated single-phase fcc FeCoNi alloy or derivative has coercivity around 100 Oe.
Excessive ordering can degrade coercive-field performance.
Complete ordering or formation of secondary phases must be avoided for the intervention to remain applicable.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends sensitively on annealing temperature and time.
XRD and TEM can verify the emergence of short-range order without full long-range order in the annealed samples.
DSC or in-situ heating can establish that the annealing parameters are below the full-order transition temperature.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to an untreated control falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary treats full ordering or secondary-phase formation as a departure from the intervention's applicability, whereas the falsification rule treats either occurrence as falsifying the hypothesis. Such an occurrence could instead indicate failure to realize the stipulated intervention.
